questions.stem: Which statement distinguishes autotrophs from heterotrophs?
options: Autotrophs do not respire; heterotrophs respire but cannot photosynthesise
Autotrophs live only in water; heterotrophs live only on land or in soil
Autotrophs make organic molecules from inorganic ones; heterotrophs consume them
Autotrophs consume organic molecules; heterotrophs make them from inorganic ones
questions.explanation: Autotrophs, such as plants, build organic compounds from carbon dioxide and water using an energy source, usually light. Heterotrophs must obtain organic compounds by consuming other organisms. Autotrophs respire too.

questions.stem: What is the main source of energy for life on Earth?
options: The sun
Glucose in the soil
Heat from the Earth's core
Oxygen in the air
questions.explanation: Most energy in living things comes from sunlight, captured by photosynthesis and passed through food webs. A few ecosystems, such as those at deep-sea vents, rely on chemical energy instead.

questions.stem: Which comparison of the inputs and outputs of a leaf cell and a muscle cell is correct?
options: Only the leaf cell can take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen overall
Only the muscle cell ever takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide
The muscle cell takes in light energy and releases glucose to the blood
The leaf cell releases nitrogenous wastes such as urea into the xylem
questions.explanation: In light, a leaf cell photosynthesises faster than it respires, so overall it takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen. Both cells respire, so both take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide at some time. Muscle cells take in glucose; they do not use light.

questions.stem: Which substances are the reactants of photosynthesis?
options: Carbon dioxide and water
Glucose and oxygen
Glucose and carbon dioxide
Oxygen and water
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water, with light energy absorbed by chlorophyll, to make glucose and oxygen. Glucose and oxygen are the reactants of aerobic respiration.

questions.stem: What is the role of photosynthesis in the transfer of energy?
options: It converts the chemical energy stored in glucose into light energy
It converts heat energy from the sun into kinetic energy
It releases energy from glucose for use by the plant cell
It converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy in the bonds of glucose. Releasing energy from glucose is the role of cellular respiration.

questions.stem: Which equation represents aerobic respiration?
options: 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2
C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy
C6H12O6 -> 2C3H6O3 + energy
C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen to carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy that is used to make ATP. The other equations show photosynthesis, fermentation in yeast and plants, and fermentation in animals.

questions.stem: How do most autotrophs and heterotrophs transform chemical energy into a form their cells can use?
options: By aerobic respiration, which transfers energy from glucose to ATP
By photosynthesis, which transfers energy from ATP to glucose
By fermentation, which transfers energy from oxygen to lactic acid
By digestion, which transfers energy from glucose to oxygen
questions.explanation: Both autotrophs and heterotrophs carry out aerobic respiration, transferring energy from glucose to ATP, which powers cell processes. Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose rather than releasing it.

questions.stem: What are the products of fermentation in yeast?
options: Glucose and oxygen
Ethanol and carbon dioxide
Lactic acid only
Water and carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Yeast and plant cells ferment glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide when oxygen is lacking. Animal cells, and some bacteria, produce lactic acid instead.

questions.stem: Which equation shows fermentation in human muscle cells?
options: C6H12O6 -> 2C3H6O3 + energy
C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy
C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy
questions.explanation: In animal cells, fermentation converts glucose to lactic acid (C3H6O3) with a small release of energy. The ethanol and carbon dioxide equation applies to yeast and plants.

questions.stem: How does the energy released from one glucose molecule by fermentation compare with that from aerobic respiration?
options: Fermentation releases much less, yielding only 2 ATP per glucose
Fermentation releases much more, because no oxygen is consumed in the process
Both release exactly the same energy, but at different speeds
Fermentation releases no energy at all; it only removes glucose
questions.explanation: Fermentation only partly breaks down glucose, producing 2 ATP per glucose, while aerobic respiration oxidises it completely to carbon dioxide and water, yielding many times more ATP. Much energy remains in the lactic acid or ethanol.

questions.stem: Yeast is grown in glucose solution in a sealed flask that initially contains air. Why does the rate of carbon dioxide production continue, but ethanol only begins to appear later?
options: Yeast respires aerobically until the oxygen is used up, then switches to fermentation
Yeast ferments first while oxygen is present, then respires aerobically once it runs out
Yeast makes ethanol only when the glucose has all been used up in the flask
Yeast cannot produce carbon dioxide by fermentation, only by aerobic respiration
questions.explanation: With oxygen present, yeast respires aerobically, producing carbon dioxide and water. Once the oxygen is used up, it switches to fermentation, producing ethanol as well as carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide output continues throughout.

questions.stem: A sprinter's muscles use fermentation during a 400 m race. Which disadvantage of relying on fermentation explains why the pace cannot be kept up for long?
options: Little ATP is made per glucose, and lactic acid builds up and lowers pH
Fermentation uses up all the oxygen in the blood, so the heart stops beating
Fermentation makes ethanol in muscle, which stops nerve impulses reaching it
Fermentation produces more carbon dioxide than the lungs can ever remove
questions.explanation: Fermentation supplies ATP quickly without oxygen, but yields only 2 ATP per glucose, and the lactic acid produced lowers the pH in muscle, contributing to fatigue. Animal cells do not make ethanol.

questions.stem: Which statement about energy and chemical bonds is correct?
options: Energy is needed both to break bonds and to form new bonds
Energy is needed to break bonds and is released when new bonds form
Energy is released when bonds break and is needed to form new bonds
Energy is released both when bonds break and when new bonds form
questions.explanation: Breaking any chemical bond requires energy, and forming a bond releases energy. A reaction releases energy overall when more energy is released by forming the new bonds than was needed to break the old ones.

questions.stem: How is ATP formed in cells?
options: Glucose joins with phosphate, using energy from ATP hydrolysis
Amino acids join together, using energy stored in fatty acids
ADP joins with inorganic phosphate, using energy from respiration
ADP is broken down further into AMP, releasing the energy needed for respiration
questions.explanation: ATP is made by adding an inorganic phosphate (Pi) to ADP, using energy released in respiration (or captured in photosynthesis). The reverse reaction, ATP to ADP + Pi, releases energy for cell processes.

questions.stem: Which cell process is directly powered by converting ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate?
options: Diffusion of oxygen into a cell across the phospholipid bilayer
Osmosis of water into a root hair cell from the soil
Facilitated diffusion of glucose down its concentration gradient
Active transport of ions against a concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Converting ATP to ADP and Pi releases energy used for processes such as active transport, muscle contraction and building large molecules. Diffusion, osmosis and facilitated diffusion are passive and need no ATP.

questions.stem: Why is ATP described as part of a cycle rather than as a long-term energy store?
options: It is stored in large amounts in fat tissue and is released only when the body is starving
It cannot be broken down by cells, so it circulates unchanged in the blood
It is made only once in each cell's life and passed to the daughter cells
It is constantly broken down to ADP and Pi and then remade, so little is stored
questions.explanation: A cell holds only a small amount of ATP, which is rapidly used and regenerated from ADP and Pi using energy from respiration. Long-term energy stores are molecules such as fats, starch and glycogen.

questions.stem: How does the folding of a mitochondrion's inner membrane into cristae help aerobic respiration?
options: It lets light reach the inside of the mitochondrion more easily
It keeps oxygen out so that fermentation can occur in the matrix
It provides a large surface area for enzymes and other proteins involved
It allows glucose to be stored between the folds until enough oxygen arrives
questions.explanation: Many reactions of aerobic respiration, including the final stage that makes most ATP, use proteins embedded in the inner membrane. Folding increases the area, so more of these proteins fit in each mitochondrion.

questions.stem: Chloroplasts contain stacks of internal membranes called thylakoids (lamellae). What is their main role?
options: They store the starch made in the light-independent reactions
They contain the circular DNA that codes for chloroplast proteins
They pump carbon dioxide into the chloroplast by active transport
They hold chlorophyll and enzymes for capturing light energy
questions.explanation: Thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll and the proteins that capture light energy, and their stacking gives a large surface area. Starch grains and chloroplast DNA are found in the surrounding fluid (stroma).

questions.stem: Mitochondria from active muscle cells have many more cristae than those from skin cells. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Muscle cells need more ATP, so a greater membrane area for respiration is an advantage
Skin cells need more ATP, so they have fewer cristae in order to slow their respiration down
Muscle cells carry out photosynthesis, so they need more internal membranes
Cristae store glucose, so muscle cells need more cristae to hold more glucose
questions.explanation: More cristae means more inner membrane and more of the proteins that make ATP, which suits cells with high energy demands such as muscle. This shows how the arrangement of internal membranes influences metabolic processes.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a metabolic pathway?
options: A route along which proteins are transported out of a cell
A set of reactions that need no enzymes because they are fast
A series of reactions, each catalysed by a specific enzyme
A single reaction that converts a substrate directly into ATP
questions.explanation: A metabolic pathway is a sequence of regulated steps, each catalysed by its own specific enzyme, with intermediate compounds produced along the way. Respiration and photosynthesis are examples.

questions.stem: Why is some energy lost as heat at each step of a metabolic pathway?
options: Enzymes absorb all the heat from the cell and store it in the substrate
Each step needs heat from outside the cell to break the enzyme apart
Heat is produced only when a pathway is blocked by an inhibitor
No energy transfer is fully efficient, so each step releases some heat
questions.explanation: In every reaction some energy is transformed into heat rather than captured in products or ATP. In mammals and birds, this heat helps maintain body temperature.

questions.stem: In the pathway A -> B -> C -> D, each step is catalysed by enzymes 1, 2 and 3 in order. A mutation makes enzyme 2 non-functional. What is expected?
options: Compound A disappears and B is converted directly to D
Compound D accumulates because enzyme 3 works faster
Compound B accumulates and little or no D is made
Compound C accumulates and D is made more quickly
questions.explanation: Enzyme 2 converts B to C. If it does not work, B builds up and C, and therefore D, cannot be made. Each step needs its own specific enzyme, so another enzyme cannot take over.

questions.stem: In many pathways, the final product inhibits the enzyme for the first step. What is the advantage of this regulation?
options: Every enzyme in the pathway is permanently destroyed after one use
The first substrate is converted into extra copies of the enzyme
Production slows when enough product is present, saving resources
Production speeds up when the product is plentiful, building reserves
questions.explanation: This negative feedback (end-product inhibition) means the pathway runs only as fast as the product is needed, avoiding wasted substrates and energy. When product levels fall, the first enzyme becomes active again.

questions.stem: Why does the rate of respiration in a reptile fall on a cold night?
options: Low temperature slows molecular collisions and enzyme activity
Low temperature denatures all of the respiratory enzymes permanently
Low temperature raises the pH in cells, so glucose cannot be used
Low temperature stops oxygen from dissolving in the blood plasma
questions.explanation: Reptiles' body temperature follows their surroundings. At low temperatures, molecules move more slowly and enzyme-substrate collisions are less frequent, so metabolic reactions slow. This is reversible, unlike denaturation at high temperature.

questions.stem: Leaf discs float as they photosynthesise. In bright light they float in 6 minutes at 0.1% carbon dioxide and in 3 minutes at 0.3%. What does this suggest?
options: Photosynthesis is slower at higher carbon dioxide concentrations
Temperature was the only factor affecting the rate of photosynthesis
Carbon dioxide concentration was limiting the rate of photosynthesis
Light intensity was limiting the rate, since carbon dioxide had no effect
questions.explanation: Raising the carbon dioxide concentration halved the time to float, so the rate increased, showing carbon dioxide was the limiting factor at 0.1% under bright light. Light and temperature would need to be kept constant for a fair test.

questions.stem: A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis rising with light intensity, then levelling off. Adding extra carbon dioxide raises the level at which it flattens. What limited the rate on the flat part of the original curve?
options: The amount of chlorophyll destroyed
The rate of respiration in the dark
Carbon dioxide concentration
Light intensity
questions.explanation: On the rising part, light is limiting. Once the curve flattens, increasing light has no effect, and raising carbon dioxide raises the plateau, so carbon dioxide was limiting there.

questions.stem: Increasing the concentration of a product can slow an enzyme-controlled reaction in a cell. Which explanation is best?
options: Product molecules can occupy or block the enzyme, reducing substrate binding
Product molecules supply extra energy that denatures the enzyme's active site completely
Product molecules change into more substrate inside the active site
Product molecules remove water from the cell by osmosis
questions.explanation: As product builds up, it can bind to the enzyme and slow the reaction, and the reverse reaction becomes more likely. This is one way metabolic pathways are regulated.

questions.stem: Cyanide blocks an enzyme used in the final stage of aerobic respiration in mitochondria. Why is cyanide so quickly lethal?
options: Cells cannot make enough ATP, so vital processes stop
Cells make far too much ATP, so they overheat and burst
Cells convert all their glucose straight into oxygen
Cells switch to photosynthesis, which uses up water
questions.explanation: Blocking the final stage of aerobic respiration stops most ATP production. Fermentation cannot supply enough ATP for organs such as the heart and brain, so cells fail rapidly.

questions.stem: The herbicide glyphosate inhibits an enzyme in a pathway plants use to make certain amino acids. Animals do not have this pathway. What does this help explain?
options: Glyphosate supplies amino acids to plants and so speeds their growth
Glyphosate inhibits every enzyme in both plants and animals equally
Glyphosate kills plants but has little direct effect on this pathway in animals
Glyphosate kills animals but has little direct effect on the growth of any plants
questions.explanation: Because the target enzyme is part of a pathway found in plants but not animals, glyphosate disrupts plant metabolism specifically. Wider effects, such as on soil organisms or non-target plants, still need to be considered.

questions.stem: Some antibiotics block bacterial ribosomes but have little effect on human ribosomes. Why can these drugs be used to treat infections?
options: They block all ribosomes equally, but bacteria are larger than human cells
They make bacteria divide faster so they use up all their glucose
They stop bacteria making proteins while human cells keep working
They stop human cells making proteins while the bacteria keep working
questions.explanation: Bacterial and human ribosomes differ in structure, so a drug can inhibit bacterial protein synthesis selectively. This disrupts bacterial metabolism and growth while human cells are largely unaffected.

questions.stem: Organophosphate insecticides inhibit an enzyme that breaks down a neurotransmitter in insects. Why must farmers handle them carefully?
options: The chemical only affects insects, so there is no risk to people or to any other species
The chemical turns into glucose in the soil and feeds harmful weeds
The chemical speeds up the enzyme in humans, so nerves stop working
The same enzyme is found in humans, so exposure can also disrupt human nerves
questions.explanation: Humans have the same enzyme in their nervous system, so organophosphates can harm people and other animals as well as insects. This shows that chemicals that interfere with metabolism can have both benefits and harmful effects.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of understanding how chemicals interfere with metabolism?
options: Chemicals can be found that increase the speed of all enzymes
Fermentation can be replaced by photosynthesis in animal cells
Drugs can be designed to inhibit enzymes found only in a pathogen
Every chemical can then be shown to be harmless to all other organisms
questions.explanation: Knowing the enzymes in a pathogen's pathways lets scientists design drugs, such as some antibiotics and antivirals, that inhibit those enzymes while sparing human cells. Unexpected side effects still need monitoring.

questions.stem: Where in a eukaryotic cell does photosynthesis take place?
options: In the chloroplasts
In the mitochondria
In the nucleus
In the ribosomes
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll on their thylakoid membranes. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.

questions.stem: Why do plant cells need mitochondria even though they have chloroplasts?
options: Mitochondria make the glucose that the chloroplasts then store as starch grains
Mitochondria absorb light at night when chloroplasts are not working
Chloroplasts need the oxygen made by mitochondria to photosynthesise
They must respire to release energy from glucose as ATP for cell processes
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, but cells need ATP to power their processes. Plant cells respire in their mitochondria, day and night, to make ATP from glucose.

questions.stem: In a sealed jar in bright light, a plant gives out oxygen. In darkness, the same plant takes in oxygen. Which explanation is correct?
options: In light, only respiration occurs; in darkness, only photosynthesis occurs
The plant respires only in the light and photosynthesises only when it is in darkness
Oxygen is absorbed in darkness because chloroplasts need it to make starch
In light, photosynthesis exceeds respiration; in darkness, only respiration occurs
questions.explanation: Plants respire all the time. In bright light, photosynthesis produces oxygen faster than respiration uses it, so there is net release. In darkness, photosynthesis stops and only respiration continues, so oxygen is taken in.
